question: What is the federal penalty for bank fraud under U.S. law?
expected_answer: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1344, whoever knowingly executes a scheme to defraud a financial institution, or to obtain money or property owned by a financial institution by means of false pretenses, can be fined or imprisoned for not more than 30 years, or both.
retrieval_context: 18 U.S.C. § 1344 — Bank fraud. Whoever knowingly executes, or attempts to execute, a scheme or artifice (1) to defraud a financial institution; or (2) to obtain any of the moneys, funds, credits, assets, securities, or other property owned by, or under the custody or control of, a financial institution, by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises; shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 30 years, or both.

question: What constitutes wire fraud under the federal criminal code?
expected_answer: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1343, wire fraud involves any person who, having devised or intending to devise any scheme or artifice to defraud, or for obtaining money or property by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, transmits or causes to be transmitted by means of wire, radio, or television communication in interstate or foreign commerce, any writings, signs, signals, pictures, or sounds. The penalty is up to 20 years imprisonment, or 30 years if the offense affects a financial institution.
retrieval_context: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 — Fraud by wire, radio, or television. Whoever, having devised or intending to devise any scheme or artifice to defraud, or for obtaining money or property by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises, transmits or causes to be transmitted by means of wire, radio, or television communication in interstate or foreign commerce, any writings, signs, signals, pictures, or sounds for the purpose of executing such scheme or artifice, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both. If the violation occurs in relation to, or involving any benefit authorized, transported, transmitted, transferred, disbursed, or paid in connection with, a presidentially declared major disaster or emergency, or affects a financial institution, such person shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 30 years, or both.

question: What is the tax treatment of contributions to a 401(k) plan?
expected_answer: Under 26 U.S.C. § 401(k), a qualified cash or deferred arrangement allows employees to elect to have the employer make contributions to a trust on behalf of the employee. These elective deferrals are not included in the employee's gross income for the year of contribution. The employer deducts the contributions, and the employee is not taxed until distribution.
retrieval_context: 26 U.S.C. § 401(k) — A qualified cash or deferred arrangement is any arrangement which is part of a profit-sharing or stock bonus plan which meets the requirements of subsection (a), or a pre-ERISA money purchase plan... Under such arrangement, each eligible employee may elect to have the employer make payments as contributions to a trust under the plan on behalf of the employee, or to the employee directly in cash. The amount an employee elects to contribute shall not be included in gross income at the time of election.

question: How does the Internal Revenue Code define 'gross income' for individual taxpayers?
expected_answer: Under 26 U.S.C. § 61, gross income means all income from whatever source derived, including but not limited to: compensation for services (including fees, commissions, fringe benefits, and similar items), gross income derived from business, gains from dealings in property, interest, rents, royalties, dividends, alimony and separate maintenance payments, annuities, income from life insurance and endowment contracts, pensions, income from discharge of indebtedness, distributive share of partnership gross income, income in respect of a decedent, and income from an interest in an estate or trust.
retrieval_context: 26 U.S.C. § 61 — Gross income defined. (a) General definition. Except as otherwise provided in this subtitle, gross income means all income from whatever source derived, including (but not limited to) the following items: (1) Compensation for services, including fees, commissions, fringe benefits, and similar items; (2) Gross income derived from business; (3) Gains derived from dealings in property; (4) Interest; (5) Rents; (6) Royalties; (7) Dividends; (8) Alimony and separate maintenance payments; (9) Annuities; (10) Income from life insurance and endowment contracts; (11) Pensions; (12) Income from discharge of indebtedness; (13) Distributive share of partnership gross income; (14) Income in respect of a decedent; and (15) Income from an interest in an estate or trust.

question: What are the general eligibility requirements for naturalization as a U.S. citizen?
expected_answer: Under 8 U.S.C. § 1427, a person may be naturalized if they: (1) have been lawfully admitted for permanent residence, (2) have resided continuously within the United States for at least five years (or three years if married to a U.S. citizen), (3) have been physically present in the U.S. for at least half of the required residency period, (4) are a person of good moral character, (5) are attached to the principles of the Constitution, and (6) are able to speak, read, and write English.

(a) No person, except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, shall be naturalized unless such applicant, (1) immediately preceding the date of filing his application for naturalization has resided continuously, after being lawfully admitted for permanent residence, within the United States for at least five years and during the five years immediately preceding the date of filing his application has been physically present therein for periods totaling at least half of that time, and who has resided within the State or within the district of the Service in the United States in which the applicant filed the application for at least three months, (2) has resided continuously within the United States from the date of the application up to the time of admission to citizenship...

expected_answer: Under 8 U.S.C. § 1227, a noncitizen who is in and has been admitted to the United States is removable if they: were inadmissible at the time of entry, violated the conditions of their admission, were convicted of certain crimes (including crimes of moral turpitude, aggravated felonies, drug offenses), committed document fraud, engaged in terrorist activities, or are subject to certain security grounds. The statute enumerates specific categories of deportable aliens.

question: What debts cannot be discharged in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy?
expected_answer: Under 11 U.S.C. § 523, debts that cannot be discharged in bankruptcy include: taxes owed to the government, debts obtained through fraud, debts for money or property obtained by false pretenses, debts for luxury goods purchased within 90 days of bankruptcy, domestic support obligations (child support and alimony), student loans (unless undue hardship is demonstrated), debts resulting from willful and malicious injury, criminal fines and penalties, and debts for driving under the influence causing injury or death.

question: What is the automatic stay in bankruptcy and what does it prohibit?
expected_answer: Under 11 U.S.C. § 362, the automatic stay is an injunction that takes effect automatically upon the filing of a bankruptcy petition. It prohibits: any act to obtain possession of or exercise control over property of the estate, any act to collect, assess, or recover a pre-petition claim, the commencement or continuation of judicial proceedings against the debtor, enforcement of any pre-petition judgment, creation or enforcement of any lien against property of the estate, and setoff of any pre-petition debt.

question: What does the Sherman Antitrust Act prohibit?
expected_answer: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1, every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal. Under 15 U.S.C. § 2, every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons to monopolize any part of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.

question: What is the federal statute of limitations for civil rights claims?
expected_answer: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1658, the statute of limitations for civil actions arising under an Act of Congress enacted after December 1, 1990, where no other limitations period is provided, is 4 years after the cause of action accrues. For civil rights claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, federal courts borrow the forum state's personal injury statute of limitations.

(a) Except as otherwise provided by law, a civil action arising under an Act of Congress enacted after the date of the enactment of this section may not be commenced later than 4 years after the cause of action accrues.

question: What are the minimum wage and overtime requirements under the Fair Labor Standards Act?
expected_answer: Under 29 U.S.C. § 206, employers must pay covered employees not less than the federal minimum wage ($7.25 per hour as of the last statutory amendment). Under 29 U.S.C. § 207, employers must compensate employees at a rate not less than one and one-half times their regular rate of pay for hours worked in excess of 40 in any workweek. Employees exempt from overtime include executive, administrative, and professional employees who meet specific salary and duties tests.

Every employer shall pay to each of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, wages at the following rates: (1) except as otherwise provided in this section, not less than—(A) $5.85 an hour, beginning on the 60th day after May 25, 2007; (B) $6.55 an hour, beginning 12 months after that 60th day; (C) $7.25 an hour, beginning 24 months after that 60th day...

question: What does Title VII of the Civil Rights Act prohibit in employment?
expected_answer: Under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2, it is unlawful for an employer to fail or refuse to hire, discharge, or otherwise discriminate against any individual with respect to compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of the individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. It is also unlawful to limit, segregate, or classify employees or applicants in ways that deprive them of employment opportunities or adversely affect their status based on these protected characteristics.
retrieval_context: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2 — Unlawful employment practices. (a) Employer practices. It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer—(1) to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin; or (2) to limit, segregate, or classify his employees or applicants for employment in any way which would deprive or tend to deprive any individual of employment opportunities or otherwise adversely affect his status as an employee, because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

question: What are the Medicare eligibility requirements under the Social Security Act?
expected_answer: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1395c, Medicare Part A hospital insurance benefits are available to individuals who are entitled to Social Security retirement benefits and are age 65 or older, individuals who have been entitled to disability benefits for at least 24 months, and individuals with end-stage renal disease who require dialysis or kidney transplant. Under 42 U.S.C. § 1395o, Medicare Part B coverage is available to individuals entitled to Part A or who are age 65 or older.

question: If a person uses a computer to commit wire fraud that also involves a financial institution, what multiple federal statutes could apply and what are the combined maximum penalties?
expected_answer: Multiple federal statutes may apply. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (wire fraud), the penalty is up to 30 years imprisonment when a financial institution is affected. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act), unauthorized computer access to commit fraud carries up to 5 years for a first offense and up to 10 years for repeat offenses. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1344 (bank fraud), if the financial institution is a federally insured bank, the penalty is up to 30 years. These charges are not mutually exclusive — a defendant can be charged under all applicable statutes, and sentences may run consecutively under 18 U.S.C. § 3584.

question: What is the federal law governing the maximum speed limit on interstate highways?
expected_answer: The U.S. Code titles covered by this system (Titles 8, 11, 15, 18, 26, 28, 29, and 42) do not contain federal provisions governing maximum highway speed limits. The National Maximum Speed Law (formerly 23 U.S.C. § 154) was repealed in 1995 by the National Highway System Designation Act, returning speed limit authority to individual states. This question cannot be answered from the available corpus.

question: Can an employer reduce an employee's hours to avoid paying overtime without violating federal law?
expected_answer: This question is ambiguous and depends on the specific facts. Under 29 U.S.C. § 207, overtime is required only for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek — reducing hours below 40 does not technically violate the FLSA overtime provision. However, under 29 U.S.C. § 215, it is unlawful to discharge or discriminate against an employee for exercising rights under the FLSA. Additionally, if the reduction targets employees who have complained about wage violations, it may constitute retaliation. The legality depends on whether the motivation is legitimate business necessity or unlawful retaliation.
retrieval_context: 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1) — No employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce...for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed. 29 U.S.C. § 215(a)(3) — it shall be unlawful for any person...to discharge or in any other manner discriminate against any employee because such employee has filed any complaint or instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding under or related to this chapter...

question: What does Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.61-1 say about the definition of gross income?
expected_answer: Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.61-1(a), gross income means all income from whatever source derived, unless excluded by law. The regulation clarifies that gross income includes income realized in any form, whether money, property, or services. Income may be realized and must be included in gross income even if the taxpayer does not receive it in cash — for example, payments made in the form of property or services are included at their fair market value.
retrieval_context: 26 C.F.R. § 1.61-1 — Gross income. (a) General definition. Gross income means all income from whatever source derived, unless excluded by law. Gross income includes income realized in any form, whether in money, property, or services. Income may be realized and thus become taxable to the taxpayer even though it is not in cash, provided that the thing of value received is of the type includible in gross income.

question: What are the Treasury Regulation requirements for a qualified 401(k) plan to satisfy the actual deferral percentage (ADP) test?
expected_answer: Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.401(k)-2, a qualified cash or deferred arrangement must satisfy the actual deferral percentage (ADP) test to avoid discrimination in favor of highly compensated employees. The ADP for eligible highly compensated employees for the plan year must not exceed the greater of: (1) 125 percent of the ADP for all other eligible employees, or (2) the lesser of 200 percent of such ADP or such ADP plus 2 percentage points. Alternatively, the plan may use the prior-year testing method or satisfy a safe harbor under section 401(k)(12) or (13).

A cash or deferred arrangement satisfies the ADP test for a plan year if— (1) The ADP for eligible highly compensated employees for the current plan year does not exceed the greater of— (i) 125 percent of the ADP of all other eligible employees for the current plan year; or (ii) The lesser of 200 percent of such ADP, or such ADP plus 2 percentage points.

question: What does 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3 say about how an eligible entity can elect its classification for federal tax purposes?
expected_answer: Under 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3, an eligible entity that is not a per se corporation can elect its federal tax classification. A domestic eligible entity with two or more members can elect to be classified as either an association taxable as a corporation or a partnership. A domestic eligible entity with a single owner can elect to be an association taxable as a corporation or to be disregarded as an entity separate from its owner. Elections are made by filing Form 8832 with the IRS, and a late election may be granted relief. The default classification applies if no election is made.

question: Under Treasury regulations, what are the requirements for a corporation to deduct compensation paid to a covered employee under 26 C.F.R. § 1.162-27?
expected_answer: Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.162-27, a publicly held corporation generally may not deduct compensation paid to a covered employee in excess of $1,000,000 per year (as limited by 26 U.S.C. § 162(m)). The regulation defines a covered employee as the chief executive officer or any employee whose total compensation is required to be reported to shareholders under the Securities Exchange Act by reason of being among the four highest compensated officers for the taxable year. The $1,000,000 limit applies to remuneration for services performed during the taxable year.

question: What does 29 C.F.R. § 541.100 say about who qualifies as an exempt executive employee under the FLSA?

question: What are the OSHA general industry requirements for employers to maintain a hazard communication program under 29 C.F.R. § 1910.1200?
expected_answer: Under 29 C.F.R. § 1910.1200 (OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard), employers must develop, implement, and maintain a written hazard communication program that includes: (1) a list of the hazardous chemicals present in the workplace; (2) procedures for labeling containers of hazardous chemicals; (3) procedures for maintaining safety data sheets (SDS) and making them accessible to employees during their work shifts; and (4) procedures for training employees on the hazards of chemicals they may be exposed to and how to protect themselves. The standard applies to any chemical that is known to be present in the workplace in such a manner that employees may be exposed under normal conditions of use.

question: Under 29 C.F.R. § 825.200, how many weeks of FMLA leave is an eligible employee entitled to, and how is the leave year calculated?
expected_answer: Under 29 C.F.R. § 825.200, an eligible employee is entitled to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during a 12-month period for FMLA-qualifying reasons. For qualifying exigency or military caregiver leave, an employee is entitled to up to 26 workweeks.

question: What does 29 C.F.R. § 778.107 say about the regular rate of pay for purposes of calculating overtime?
expected_answer: Under 29 C.F.R. § 778.107, the regular rate of pay is the hourly rate actually paid to the employee for the normal, non-overtime workweek. The regular rate is an hourly rate, and it must be derived from the total straight-time compensation paid to the employee during the workweek divided by the total number of hours actually worked. It cannot be a rate arbitrarily chosen by the employer — it must reflect the actual compensation paid for the hours worked.

question: What are the Treasury Regulation rules under 26 C.F.R. § 1.704-1 for determining whether a partnership's allocation of income or loss has substantial economic effect?
expected_answer: Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.704-1(b)(2), an allocation has economic effect only if the partnership agreement provides for: (1) the maintenance of capital accounts in accordance with the regulations; (2) liquidation of each partner's interest in accordance with positive capital account balances; and (3) an unconditional obligation for partners with deficit capital accounts to restore the deficit after liquidation (or an alternative test using a qualified income offset). Economic effect is 'substantial' if there is a reasonable possibility that the allocation will affect substantially the dollar amounts to be received by the partners from the partnership, independent of tax consequences.

question: What does 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2 say about the definition of 'disability' for purposes of the ADA regulations?
expected_answer: Under 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(g), disability means, with respect to an individual: (1) a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more of the major life activities of such individual; (2) a record of such an impairment; or (3) being regarded as having such an impairment. Part 541 then supply the specific tests: 29 C.F.R. § 541.100 requires executive employees to be paid a salary of at least $684/week, have management as their primary duty, direct two or more employees, and have hiring/firing authority. 29 C.F.R. § 541.200 requires administrative employees to have primary duties of office or non-manual work directly related to management or general business operations and to exercise discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance. 29 C.F.R. § 541.300 requires professional employees to have primary duties requiring advanced knowledge in a field of science or learning, customarily acquired by a prolonged course of specialized intellectual instruction.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in United States v. Skilling about the scope of 'honest services' fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1346?
expected_answer: In United States v. Skilling, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), the Supreme Court held that 18 U.S.C. § 1346's prohibition on honest services fraud is limited to bribery and kickback schemes. The Court declined to extend the statute to cover undisclosed self-dealing by a corporate officer, finding that such an expansive reading would render the statute unconstitutionally vague. The Court narrowed § 1346 by construing it to reach only the bribery-and-kickback core of honest-services prosecutions that had been consistently charged before the statute's enactment. The decision vacated Skilling's honest-services conviction and required remand to determine whether his securities fraud conviction could stand independently.

Skilling, 561 U.S. 358 (2010) — The Supreme Court held that 18 U.S.C. § 1346, which extends the wire fraud statute to cover deprivation of 'honest services,' is limited to bribery and kickback schemes. To avoid unconstitutional vagueness, the Court construed the statute narrowly: 'A limiting construction is thus necessary... and we find it in the bribery and kickback core of § 1346.' Undisclosed self-dealing by a corporate insider does not satisfy § 1346 as construed. The Court vacated Skilling's honest-services conviction and remanded.

question: Under McDonnell v. United States, what constitutes an 'official act' for purposes of federal bribery under 18 U.S.C. § 201, and what conduct does not qualify?
expected_answer: In McDonnell v. United States, 579 U.S. 550 (2016), the Supreme Court held that an 'official act' under 18 U.S.C. § 201(a)(3) requires a formal exercise of governmental power on a 'question, matter, cause, suit, proceeding or controversy' that is pending or may be brought before the official. The official must make a decision or take action on the pending matter — not merely facilitate access to other officials. Arranging meetings with government officials, calling another public official, or hosting an event does not, standing alone, constitute an official act. The Court reversed Governor McDonnell's conviction because the jury instructions had permitted conviction based on actions that did not meet this standard.
retrieval_context: McDonnell v. United States, 579 U.S. 550 (2016) — The Supreme Court held that 18 U.S.C. § 201's 'official act' element requires a formal exercise of governmental power on a pending question or matter. Chief Justice Roberts wrote: 'Setting up a meeting, calling another official, or hosting an event does not, standing alone, qualify as an official act.' The defendant must make a decision or take action on the matter itself, not merely open doors to other officials. The Court reversed and remanded McDonnell's conviction, finding the jury instructions allowed too broad a definition of official act.

question: What three-part test did the Supreme Court establish in Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co. for determining gross income under 26 U.S.C. § 61, and does it cover punitive damages?
expected_answer: In Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co., 348 U.S. 426 (1955), the Supreme Court established that gross income under 26 U.S.C. § 61 encompasses all 'undeniable accessions to wealth, clearly realized, and over which the taxpayers have complete dominion.' Applying this three-part test, the Court held that punitive damages and treble damages received in antitrust and fraud settlements are includable in gross income because they constitute accessions to wealth that the taxpayer has clearly realized and over which the taxpayer exercises complete dominion. The Court rejected the argument that gross income was limited to compensation for services or proceeds from capital transactions, affirming Congress's intent to tax all gains except those specifically exempted.
retrieval_context: Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co., 348 U.S. 426 (1955) — The Supreme Court held that punitive damages received in antitrust and fraud litigation constitute gross income under the Internal Revenue Code. The Court articulated: 'Here we have instances of undeniable accessions to wealth, clearly realized, and over which the taxpayers have complete dominion.' This three-part standard superseded earlier narrow interpretations and reflected Congress's intent 'to tax all gains except those specifically exempted.' The Court reversed the Tax Court's ruling that punitive damages were not taxable income.

question: What standard did the Supreme Court establish in Welch v. Helvering for determining whether a business expense is 'ordinary and necessary' under 26 U.S.C. § 162, and why were the payments disallowed?
expected_answer: In Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111 (1933), the Supreme Court held that for a business expense to be 'ordinary' under § 162, it must be normal, usual, or customary in the relevant trade or calling. Justice Cardozo observed that 'ordinary' is a relative term whose meaning depends on the practices of others in the same field. The payments at issue — voluntary payments by Welch to discharge the debts of his former employer in order to restore business relationships — were deemed extraordinary because no reasonable businessman in that industry would feel obligated to pay another's debts. The Court also found the payments were capital expenditures for goodwill rather than deductible current expenses, since their benefit extended beyond the tax year.

Justice Cardozo wrote: 'Now, what is ordinary, though there must always be a strain of constancy within it, is none the less a variable affected by time and place and circumstance.' Paying another's debts to rebuild business goodwill is extraordinary, not ordinary. The Court held the payments were capital expenditures for goodwill rather than deductible ordinary and necessary business expenses under what is now 26 U.S.C. § 162.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Nobelman v. American Savings Bank about a Chapter 13 debtor's ability to modify a residential mortgage under 11 U.S.C. § 1322(b)(2)?
expected_answer: In Nobelman v. American Savings Bank, 508 U.S. 324 (1993), the Supreme Court held that 11 U.S.C. § 1322(b)(2) prohibits a Chapter 13 debtor from bifurcating an undersecured residential mortgage into secured and unsecured components and reducing the mortgage to the property's market value. The anti-modification clause of § 1322(b)(2) protects a lender whose claim is secured only by a security interest in the debtor's principal residence. Even when the outstanding mortgage debt exceeds the property's current market value, the lender's full contractual rights — including the right to full repayment, interest rate, and foreclosure rights — cannot be modified through the Chapter 13 plan. The debtor cannot use § 506(a)'s bifurcation mechanism to circumvent the anti-modification protection.

American Savings Bank, 508 U.S. 324 (1993) — The Supreme Court held that § 1322(b)(2) protects residential mortgage lenders from having their contractual rights modified in a Chapter 13 plan, even when the property is worth less than the debt. Justice Thomas wrote: 'The Court of Appeals correctly held that § 1322(b)(2) prohibits petitioners from relying on § 506(a) to reduce the outstanding mortgage principal to the fair market value of their residence.' The anti-modification clause encompasses the bank's full bundle of rights as the holder of a claim secured only by the debtor's principal residence.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in RadLAX Gateway Hotel v. Amalgamated Bank about a secured creditor's right to credit bid in a Chapter 11 cramdown plan under 11 U.S.C. § 1129(b)?
expected_answer: In RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639 (2012), the Supreme Court unanimously held that a Chapter 11 debtor who seeks to sell collateral free and clear of liens through a cramdown plan must permit the secured creditor to credit bid under 11 U.S.C. § 1129(b)(2)(A)(ii). The debtor had argued it could avoid the credit-bid requirement by invoking the more general 'indubitable equivalent' clause in § 1129(b)(2)(A)(iii) instead. The Court rejected this argument by applying the canon that a specific provision governs over a general one: the sale provision in subclause (ii) specifically requires credit bidding for asset sales, and a debtor cannot circumvent that requirement by invoking the catch-all subclause (iii). This ruling confirmed that secured creditors retain a non-waivable right to credit bid whenever their collateral is sold through a plan.

retrieval_context: RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639 (2012) — The Supreme Court unanimously held that a Chapter 11 cramdown plan that sells collateral must allow the secured creditor to credit bid under § 1129(b)(2)(A)(ii). Justice Scalia wrote for the Court: 'The specific provision governs the general: a debtor who proposes to sell its assets under a plan must permit secured creditors to credit bid, and cannot satisfy § 1129(b)(2)(A) by instead providing the indubitable equivalent.' The debtor could not use the general subclause (iii) to bypass the credit-bidding requirement of the specific subclause (ii).

question: What was the constitutional significance of NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp. for the validity of the National Labor Relations Act under 29 U.S.C. § 151?
expected_answer: In NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 301 U.S. 1 (1937), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the National Labor Relations Act under the Commerce Clause of Article I, Section 8. The Court held that labor relations at a nationally integrated steel producer substantially affected interstate commerce, giving Congress authority to regulate unfair labor practices. Chief Justice Hughes rejected the previously applied distinction between 'direct' and 'indirect' effects on commerce, adopting a practical economic test instead. The decision validated federal protection of workers' rights to organize and bargain collectively under 29 U.S.C. § 157 and the NLRA's prohibition of unfair labor practices under § 158, effectively establishing the constitutional foundation for modern federal labor law.
expected_citation: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel, 301 U.S. 1 (1937)
retrieval_context: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 301 U.S. 1 (1937) — The Supreme Court upheld the NLRA as a valid exercise of Congress's commerce power. Chief Justice Hughes wrote: 'When industries organize themselves on a national scale, making their relation to interstate commerce the dominant factor in their activities, how can it be maintained that their industrial labor relations constitute a forbidden field into which Congress may not enter?' The Court held that labor strife at a vertically integrated national steel company substantially affected interstate commerce, sustaining the NLRA's protections for employee organizing and collective bargaining.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis about the enforceability of class action waivers in employment arbitration agreements under the NLRA and the Federal Arbitration Act?
expected_answer: In Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. 497 (2018), the Supreme Court held in a 5-4 decision that employment arbitration agreements requiring individual arbitration and prohibiting class or collective actions must be enforced under the Federal Arbitration Act. The employees had argued that class action waivers violated § 7 of the NLRA (29 U.S.C. § 157), which guarantees the right to engage in concerted activities for mutual aid and protection. The Court rejected this, holding that: (1) the FAA requires enforcement of arbitration agreements according to their terms; (2) § 7 of the NLRA does not clearly prohibit individual arbitration agreements with class action waivers; and (3) the FAA's savings clause only preserves generally applicable contract defenses, not rules that single out arbitration agreements for disfavored treatment.
retrieval_context: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. 497 (2018) — The Supreme Court held that employment arbitration agreements containing class action waivers are enforceable under the FAA and that the NLRA's § 7 does not create an exception. Justice Gorsuch wrote: 'The FAA requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements and class action waivers like any other contract. The NLRA does not expressly mention arbitration agreements and nothing in its legislative history suggests Congress meant to displace the FAA.' The Court resolved a circuit split, ruling that the right to concerted activities under § 7 does not include a right to class or collective litigation procedures.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Chevron U.S.A. v. Echazabal about the ADA's direct threat defense when the threat is to the employee's own health rather than to coworkers?
expected_answer: In Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Echazabal, 536 U.S. 73 (2002), the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the EEOC's regulation extending the ADA's direct threat defense to threats to the employee's own health, even though 42 U.S.C. § 12113(b) by its terms covers threats to the health or safety of 'other individuals in the workplace.' The Court applied Chevron deference and held that the EEOC's extension was a permissible construction of the ADA because: (1) the statute did not unambiguously address whether self-directed threats were covered; and (2) the EEOC's interpretation was reasonable in light of the ADA's overall purposes and employer safety interests. An employer could therefore refuse to hire Echazabal because his liver condition would have been worsened by exposure to refinery chemicals.

Echazabal, 536 U.S. 73 (2002) — The Supreme Court upheld the EEOC's regulation extending the ADA direct threat defense to threats to the employee himself, despite the statutory text of 42 U.S.C. § 12113(b) referring only to threats to 'other individuals in the workplace.' Justice Souter wrote: 'Here, the EEOC has applied the direct threat defense to threats to others and extended it to threats to the employee as well... Nothing in the statute bars this extension.' The Court found the EEOC's expansion a reasonable interpretation of the statute entitled to Chevron deference.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Olmstead v. L.C. about states' obligations under Title II of the ADA to provide community-based services to persons with mental disabilities?
expected_answer: In Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999), the Supreme Court held that unjustified institutionalization of persons with mental disabilities constitutes discrimination under Title II of the ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12132). States are required to provide community-based services when: (1) the state's treatment professionals determine that community placement is appropriate; (2) the transfer is not opposed by the affected individual; and (3) the placement can be reasonably accommodated, taking into account the state's resources and the needs of others with mental disabilities. This is the 'integration mandate.' States must have a comprehensive, effectively working plan for placing qualified persons in less restrictive settings and must demonstrate reasonable movement toward that goal.

L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999) — The Supreme Court held that Title II of the ADA, 42 U.S.C. § 12132, requires states to provide community-based services to persons with mental disabilities when appropriate, not opposed by the individual, and reasonably accommodable. Justice Ginsburg wrote: 'States are required to provide community-based services to persons with mental disabilities when the State's treatment professionals determine that such placement is appropriate, the transfer is not opposed by the affected individual, and the placement can be reasonably accommodated, taking into account the resources available to the State and the needs of others with mental disabilities.' The ADA integration regulation at 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d) reinforces this mandate.

question: What does 18 U.S.C. § 1346 say about honest services fraud on its face, and how did the Supreme Court in United States v. Skilling narrow the statute's reach in a way that diverges from the plain text?

The statutory text is broad and on its face could reach any breach of fiduciary duty or undisclosed self-dealing. However, in United States v. Skilling, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), the Supreme Court held that § 1346 must be limited — to avoid unconstitutional vagueness — to only bribery and kickback schemes. The Court explicitly rejected prosecutorial theories based on undisclosed self-dealing, even though such conduct plausibly falls within the statute's plain language. There is genuine tension here: § 1346's text is broad enough to encompass self-dealing by corporate officers, but Skilling's narrowing construction means prosecutors must rely on the Court's limiting gloss rather than the statutory text alone when charging honest-services fraud.

The Court vacated Skilling's honest-services conviction. The statute's text reaches broadly; Skilling's construction reaches only narrowly.

question: How does 26 U.S.C. § 61's definition of gross income relate to the standard from Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co., and does the case expand, restrict, or simply apply the statute?

Rather than conflicting with § 61, Glenshaw Glass is entirely consistent with the statute — it supplies the analytical framework for applying § 61's intentionally expansive mandate to income types not enumerated in the list. The Court held that punitive damages satisfy all three prongs and are therefore gross income. Case and statute are aligned: Glenshaw Glass explains how to apply § 61, not how to limit or extend it beyond its text.

question: How does 11 U.S.C. § 1322(b)(2)'s anti-modification clause apply to residential mortgages, and what did Nobelman v. American Savings Bank hold about its scope in an undersecured mortgage situation?

In Nobelman v. American Savings Bank, 508 U.S. 324 (1993), the Supreme Court applied this provision and held that even when a residential mortgage is undersecured — meaning the property's value is less than the outstanding balance — the lender's contractual rights cannot be bifurcated or reduced through a Chapter 13 plan. The statute and case are consistent: Nobelman applies § 1322(b)(2) as written, declining to allow debtors to use § 506(a)'s bifurcation rule to circumvent the anti-modification protection. Both the statute and the Court's interpretation protect residential mortgage lenders from modification, creating a notable carve-out from the general rule that secured claims can be crammed down.

question: What rights does 29 U.S.C. § 157 guarantee to employees, and how did NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp. validate Congress's power to enforce those rights through federal law?

The Court found that labor relations at a nationally integrated steel producer substantially affected interstate commerce, giving Congress the authority to prohibit unfair labor practices and protect the rights enumerated in § 157. The statute and case are fully consistent: Jones & Laughlin confirmed the constitutional foundation that makes § 157's guarantees enforceable through the NLRB, and the decision did not narrow or restrict the statutory rights.

question: How does 42 U.S.C. § 12113(b)'s direct threat defense read on its face, and how does Chevron U.S.A. v. Echazabal diverge from the statute's plain text in extending the defense to threats to the employee?
